item.title: Achakzai sees governor's rule next being imposed in Sindh, over water and mines
item.description:
Opposition Leader in the National Assembly Mehmood Khan Achakzai warned on Wednesday that governor’s rule would be imposed next in Sindh over the “occupation of water, mines and streams”, urging the Centre to give provinces their rights and resources.

He was speaking in the National Assembly, where a resolution endorsing the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Sunday was passed. The federal government cited the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism as the reason for imposing governor’s rule in KP.

In days preceding the development, political tensions between the federal government and the opposition, mainly the PTI, had remained high after the party announced a long march to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. However, the march, initially planned for Islamabad, remained confined to KP until it fizzled out with the imposition of governor’s rule in the province.

In his address, Achakzai said KP’s “mistake is that it saved itself with the help of its people”. He also drew a comparison between the current situation with regards to KP and the one witnessed at the time of the creation of Bangladesh.

He also assailed the government for depriving the PTI of its election symbol ahead of the 2024 general elections. “And the mistake of his (Imran’s) party’s workers was that they contested the elections on 200 different symbols and turned your own game around on you. You are meting out the punishment for that? You are punishing 240 million people of Pakistan for that?”

The opposition leader also pointed out that Sohail Afridi, who has become non-functional as the chief minister after the imposition of governor’s rule and had been leading the PTI’s march, had not resorted to violence or using expletives in his call for the protest.

He went on to say, “When you try to snatch our right to self-determination, our right to vote, we all will stand against you. All of us, all provinces.”

Noting the participation of the PPP, which is in power in Sindh, Achakzai said it pained him. He then warned that governor’s rule would next be imposed in Sindh over the “occupation of water, mines and streams”.

“And then you will recall your mistake,” he said, noting however that there was still time to rectify mistakes.

“Reverse these decisions,” Achakzai said, urging that Parliament be made the centre of power. “And Pakistan will be saved.”

He warned that when the “state turns against its own people, they are compelled to look elsewhere”.

The opposition also criticised the government over the country’s economic situation.

“You are looting this country’s resources […] Have some mercy on this country. […] This country is drowning because of our mistakes. There is only one way to save it: through its Constitution and Parliament and by having a democratic system,” he asserted.

Achakzai also lamented the fact the Parliament was not taken into confidence over decisions related to foreign affairs, and that Pakistan had strained ties with most of its neighbours.

On Imran, who has not been allowed meetings with his family and associates for a long time, Achakzai said: “Which provision of the Constitution … places a restriction on meetings with the most popular leader of the country?”

He assured that if meetings were arranged with Imran, “we will just try to assess his health condition and will try to resolve matter between you. We promise we will meet him and not tell anyone. […] Have some sense. Negotiate.”

He concluded his address by declaring that the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP was wrong.

item.title: National Assembly, Senate pass resolutions endorsing Centre's imposition of emergency in KP
item.description:
ISLAMABAD: Shortly after the National Assembly passed a resolution endorsing the federal government’s imposition of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Wednesday, the Senate also gave its approval for the measure.

The Centre had imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Sunday, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and the PTI after the latter announced a long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan.

Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry tabled the motions regarding the proclamation of emergency before both Houses.

Senate proceedings

In the Senate, the resolution was passed amid the opposition’s outcry, with PTI senators staging a walkout.

The Senate’s approval followed a heated debate between treasury and opposition members, during which Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar defended the procedural propriety presenting the resolution in the House and getting it approved.

He argued that a “constitutional resolution” had been laid before the House in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Senate. “Under Article 232, a copy of [the proclamation of] emergency has been laid before the House. An attempt to bypass the constitutional procedure cannot succeed,” he said, adding that the requirement of a seven-day notice for tabling a resolution did not apply to one presented under a constitutional necessity.

“If its opponents have any objections, they should reject the resolution through their vote after the debate. We cannot deviate from the Constitution and rules of the House,” he said.

As opposition voiced opposition to the resolution, Senate Chairperson Yousuf Raza Gilani asked them to exercise patience. “This is not a classroom, do not make noise,” he remarked as senators from the opposition benches continued sloganeering.

Among them, PTI’s Humayun Mohmand said independent Senator Faisal Vawda had said months ago that governor’s rule would be imposed. He alleged that terrorism being cited as the reason for the measure was just an excuse and the actual “target is the PTI”.

“The decision to impose governor’s rule and emergency was taken months ago,” he alleged. Seemingly referring to the creation of Bangladesh, he said the federal government’s decision since 1970 had proved wrong.

PTI-backed Senator Hamid Khan also argued that there “seems to be some other objectives behind governor’s rule and emergency”. Referring to the talks between the Centre and the opposition ahead of governor’s rule and emergency in KP, he alleged that negotiations “were just a drama” and were held “only to deceive the people”.

“The real decision was taken elsewhere long ago,” he claimed. He further said that Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam Fazl chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who tried to mediate between the Centre and the opposition, had stated that while the negotiations were taking place, “a decision came”.

“Governments formed on the basis of Form-47 do not have the real mandate,” he added.

He further regretted that after the 26th Amendment, “there is neither any Constitution nor an independent judicial system”.

“The judiciary has been stripped of its independence, which closes the avenues to challenge unconstitutional steps,” he said.

Khan went on to say: “Article 232 has to be presented before the House for debate, not just for saying yes. Decision was taken by those whom Constitution does not allow to take the decision, but they have complete dominance over Constitution. At this time, neither is there any Constitution nor any court in the country.”

PTI Senator Mohsin Aziz railed against federal ministers, who have been accusing the PTI of facilitating terrorism.

“You talk about terrorism, what do you know about terrorism? People of KP sacrificed their children and picked up bodies. […] Did we support Pakistan or terrorists? Those calling people of KP terrorists should be ashamed. These are valiant people who saved this country,” he said.

Aziz said terrorism was a result of unemployment, hunger, non-availability of hospitals, water and education.

Senator Zeeshan Khanzada, also from the PTI, said he condemned the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP. He accused the federal government of “abducting” Sohail Afridi, who has been rendered non-functional as the KP chief minister following the imposition of governor’s rule, and other PTI MPAs.

JUI-F’s Kamran Murtaza said the opposition’s resolution against governor’s rule should have also been included in the agenda for the day, but it was returned with objections.

Murtaza argued that the relevant material required for endorsement of enforcement of Article 232 and 234 — constitutional provision related to imposition of emergency and governor’s rule — had not been presented in the House.

Despite letters and applications, the government had not provided documents and material related to the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule, he said, adding that senators had to obtain that material through social media.

Members could not be satisfied with a decision until complete information came forth, he said.

NA proceedings

The NA question hour session was suspended due to discussions on the emergency. The motion in the lower House of Parliament was adopted with a majority vote after a discussion opened by Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar.

“The National Assembly approves the Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President on the 11th October, 2026 in the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under second proviso of clause (1) of Article 232 of the Constitution,” read a post by NA’s official X account.

According to Article 232, if the “president acts on his own, the Proclamation of Emergency shall be placed” before both Houses of the Parliament for approval by each House within 10 days.

Meanwhile, a proclamation for governor’s rule issued under Article 234 “shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months”, unless a joint sitting approves its extension. However, such a measure shall not remain in force for more than six months.

Throughout Wednesday’s proceedings, opposition members participated calmly and did not stage any loud protest, unlike past instances when the PTI objects to the Centre.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also attended part of the session, with pictures released by the NA showing him shaking hands with Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai.

Federal ministers defended the emergency imposition while assailing what they described as the PTI-led KP government’s lack of will to combat terrorism.

In tune with that, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari blamed the PTI for the circumstances that compelled the Centre to impose emergency in KP and termed it a “political suicide attack” for the party.

However, he also urged the treasury and the opposition to get back on the path of dialogue and make joint efforts against terrorism.

At one point during the proceedings, NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq noted that the Oct 3 dialogue was held in a cordial atmosphere.

Sadiq praised both sides for “attempting more than their capacity so that the matter is settled”.

However, he said some matters were beyond the parties’ control and voiced his support for forming the same committees for negotiations if ever needed in the future.

Addressing PTI lawmakers, the speaker said, “Everyone’s response was that this [process of dialogue] should continue, but you also understand that your hands were tied.”

He took note of the PTI’s complaints regarding the jail conditions of party founder Imran Khan, adding that he had even provided details of facilities provided to the jailed ex-premier.

The session was adjourned to meet again at 11am on Oct 16 (Friday).

‘Political suicide attack’

Bilawal began his speech by highlighting that emergency and governor’s rule in KP were measures taken under the Constitution. Reading the relevant provisions, he asserted that the Centre tried its best to “engage the opposition so this step did not have to be taken”.

“They will have to accept, even if not publicly, but the responsible leadership of the opposition knows that the PTI itself carried out a political suicide attack on its KP government,” he remarked.

The PPP chief maintained that the PTI could not deny that its “leadership, particularly in the province had a key role in the political, constitutional and legal circumstances” at present.

Bilawal emphasised that the PPP’s stance was that “before employing this constitutional atomic bomb, we must engage with PTI and the opposition and try to address the federal government’s reservations that they were not supporting them in the war against terrorism”.

He observed: “If political space is restricted for one political party, it is impossible that it remains restricted for that particular party; it is limited for every political party, political worker and Pakistani citizen.

“We are responsible for this, but you cannot deny that you are also responsible for it,” he said.

Terming the imposition of emergency a “difficult decision”, Bilawal recalled alleged remarks by Sohail Afridi — the KP chief minister whose role is now non-functional — that he would not combat terrorism the way the Centre wanted.

“If this was not a political suicide, then what else was it?”

The Bhutto scion wondered if the opposition and Afridi had left any reason for President Asif Ali Zardari, who he said prides himself on passing the 18th Amendment, to “refuse to sign” the emergency proclamation.

He argued that due to the PTI’s actions and statements, neither the president, the Centre, nor he had any legal or political reason left for not imposing emergency in KP.

“But even today, I would recommend to the federal government that we extend our hand forward once again for negotiations, political discussions and try to find a resolution and a middle path,” Bilawal added.

The PPP chairman noted that emergency was “always a stopgap measure”.

“We cannot sustain the emergency forever,” he added, emphasising that while the counterterrorism fight would be better than before, an “all-of-society and all-of-country response” was needed to eradicate it completely.

Regarding the Oct 3 talks of a joint delegation of the PPP and the government with the opposition, Bilawal said, “Late at night, I was informed that congratulations, negotiations are succeeding.”

He said the PTI was willing to declare the areas in KP with surging terrorism as “terrorist areas”, and the opposition was about to agree that the federal and KP governments would sign a pact on joint efforts against terrorism. However, the dialogue collapsed.

The former foreign minister pointed out that the security challenges Pakistan was facing were “way more complicated” than before, adding that India “could still not digest […] its embarrassment” from the May 2025 conflict.

Referring to remarks by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi that its ‘Operation Sindoor’ was still ongoing, Bilawal said: “It means that India is still sponsoring terrorist incidents in Pakistan, sometimes in the form of TTP (Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan) and sometimes in the form of separatist terrorist groups.”

He reiterated Pakistan’s stance that India was involved in terrorist activities being conducted from across the Afghan border.

The ex-foreign minister then highlighted Islamabad’s role as a mediator in the US-Iran war.

“But there is a state — which we do not recognise as a state — that will neither be happy nor ever forget that you took this step. And those Zionist forces will and are interfering in Pakistan’s internal politics and state.”

Concluding his speech, the PPP chairman emphasised the need for building consensus on “some fundamental issues” for an empowered lower house.

“Even today, we are saying, come and at least begin from this house,” he said while addressing the opposition benches.

Gohar demands implementation of NAP

Speaking in the NA, PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan said his party “rejected” the Centre’s move to impose emergency in KP.

He asked what “terrorism” Imran’s wife or sisters had allegedly been involved in that they had been put behind bars, or what the accusations were against the PTI MNAs and MPAs who he said were detained.

Gohar further said, “One person is not present in the house currently. When he comes during a joint session, then I will reveal the reality of the negotiations.”

He affirmed that the PTI had raised its voice against terrorism, adding that measures against the scourge must be taken according to the National Action Plan (NAP).

Gohar argued that the PML-N opposition during the PTI’s tenure carried out “14 long marches in two years, but you did not let us stage even one long march”.

Presenting his version of the Oct 3 talks with the government, the PTI leader said his party was being asked to immediately call off the long march. “I said where did [the topic] of terrorism arise from suddenly.”

Noting that the government had put forward “five reservations”, Gohar said PTI was willing to make the KP Police Act similar to that of Punjab and Sindh.

The PTI leader reiterated his party’s request for the production of certain MNAs it says were taken into custody.

Gohar also welcomed Bilawal’s proposal to continue dialogue.

Responding to Gohar’s remarks, the PPP chairman said the PTI was busy in its long march while the people of KP were being targeted by terrorists.

Bilawal reiterated that the opposition could keep arguing against the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, but no one could deny that the decision was grounded in the Constitution.

“I cannot insist on the government to continue talks with PTI despite being defrauded multiple times,” the PPP chairman said.

Pointing towards Gohar and Achakzai, Bilawal said: “I believe that none of them is allied with terrorists. I believe that they will definitely want to combat terrorism; however, they cannot deny the fact that their former chief minister contradicted this fact.”

Bilawal again requested all the stakeholders to unite and combat terrorism collectively. He also called for the provision of all facilities to the incarcerated PTI founder.

‘Threat to national security’

Addressing the house, the law minister explained that emergency was imposed in KP as the security situation there was becoming a threat to “national security”.

Tarar noted that after the Proclamation of Emergency was issued, the Constitution’s Article 232 required that both houses of the parliament approve the measure.

He recalled that the federal cabinet examined “material” regarding terrorism in the province during its Oct 11 meeting and then advised PM Shehbaz to recommend the imposition of emergency.

He noted that some people compared the measure to the emergency imposed by former dictator Gen Pervez Musharraf on Oct 12, 1999.

The minister particularly noted “internal disturbances” and cross-border infiltrations. He contended that the situation since Oct 15, 2025, when Sohail Afridi’s government came into power in KP, was “turning into a threat to national security to an alarming extent”.

He went on to highlight that there was a rise in terrorism in KP, especially after 2021, due to the approach of the provincial government.

“Perhaps there might be foreign, diplomatic and political reasons behind it, which got inflamed due to a political party’s point of view.”

Tarar stated that 2,911 incidents of terrorism took place between 2021 and 2024 in KP, but they surged to 3,787 incidents between Oct 15, 2025 and Oct 9, 2026.

He criticised the KP chief minister for ignoring martyred security and police personnel, and for instead preferring to promote his political designs and make visits across the country.

“Even this was announced that the federal capital will be conquered,” he said, referring to the party’s plan to hold a protest long march towards the federal capital.

The PML-N leader expressed his government’s gratitude to NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq for providing a platform for dialogue between the Centre and the opposition. He reiterated the government’s stance that the PTI had the agreement draft changed multiple times, but even then backed off from it.

Tarar observed that the PTI demanded the release of their party founder Imran Khan and his treatment in a private hospital despite knowing that only courts could provide such a relief.

He said two days would be “remembered in the country’s democratic history with regard to misfortune and a political party”.

On the emergency measure, the law minister noted that a special mechanism has been introduced for 12 districts of KP.

Speaking after Tarar, Achakzai criticised him for trying to prove that terrorism was not tackled in KP.

The opposition leader questioned the government’s mandate in the February 2024 general elections, quipping that the opposition would “surrender” if the minister could swear that the government won those polls fairly.

Achakzai alleged that the incumbent ruling coalition was formed “illegally”.

‘You do not have clean hands’

Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif went on to recall the tenure of the PTI government in the Centre and assailed the party’s past actions.

Referring to ex-prime minister Imran Khan’s plan to resettle members of the TTP, he said PTI tried to convince the then-opposition that “bringing these terrorists back would be better for Pakistan”.

The PML-N leader mentioned the 2019 episode of an Indian pilot’s capture in Pakistan: “They had threatened and we were surrendering. The then-prime minister was saying, ‘What should I do? Attack India?’”

Asif urged the opposition to reflect on its past actions, adding that Imran often used to praise former army chief retired General Qamar Javed Bajwa.

“As long as this contradiction remains in our words and actions and in our society, the circumstances of this country will not fix.”

He narrated his time behind bars during the PTI government, when Shehbaz “smuggled a blanket” to him to brace the low temperatures. “I used to eat the jail’s food,” he said, claiming that orders were given to remove the geyser when it was installed.

“But we did not hold rallies or mourn at D-Chowk or dig graves. We did not martyr police and law enforcement personnel,” Asif remarked.

“You demand equity when you have clean hands. You do not have clean hands, you cannot demand equity; this is a thousand-year-old principle,” he contended.

“You know very well what Gen Musharraf did to me. There was a 4x6 cell in Attock jail,” the PML-N politician said, emphasising that he stood with his party and ex-PM Nawaz Sharif.

Speaking on the current political situation, Asif alleged that Afridi used to “take directives […] from a person sitting in Afghanistan”.

He referred to a statement by the TTP condemning the imposition of emergency and deployment of troops in certain places. “Who is their ally and who is their rival?” he said.

The minister further countered the PTI’s stance that its leaders have not been able to meet Imran, who is imprisoned in the Adiala jail. “Meetings are held, [but] a lot of them are not publicised or brought on record,” he maintained.

Farooq Sattar urges PTI to ‘openly condemn terrorism’

In his remarks on the floor of the lower house, Farooq Sattar expressed Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan’s (MQM-P) confidence in the decision taken by the prime minister.

“This was an extremely difficult decision, but so unavoidable that you had no other option,” Sattar said about imposing emergency and governor’s rule.

“We trust your decision as we trust your experience, capabilities, political acumen, and that you made this decision in the interest of the nation,” he added.

The MQM-P lawmaker contended that the PTI was “on the wrong side and does not have concrete arguments” to declare that the decision was baseless or made with political motives.

“The main issue is of the mindset,” he declared, adding that Imran had “publicly said that the war on terror is not ours”. “This is their policy. This is their mindset.”

Sattar questioned whether the KP government had ever published reports to expose terrorist hideouts and extremist trends. He further raised questions about the government’s pursuit of cases against suspected terrorists.

“Openly condemn terrorism; else, the allegation of backing [it], if a commission is formed and God forbid, it is proven in the inquiry that there is political extremism and terrorism complicity, there is a nexus, then where will you go?”

Sattar recounted his past MQM experiences, saying, “I have also suffered such times. A lot of times, the narrative coming from the top was difficult to defend. Today, I feel that Barrister Gohar is also not in the position to defend his [party’s] position on KP.”

item.title: Top leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party sent to jail after protest
item.description:
Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were remanded in custody for five days on Wednesday, as police ratcheted up efforts to clamp down on anti-election commission protests.

CJP activists and opposition parties have defied a security crackdown to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.

The commission, which oversees voting in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.

Delhi police said CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, 30, and Saurav Das, 27, were taken into custody for their “alleged repeated attempts to disturb public peace and violate the law”.

At the end of the five-day remand period, they could have their detention extended, be granted bail or be released.

On Tuesday, the pair jumped security barricades to wave the national flag at Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have barred people from using.

“Their alleged attempts to instigate others through social media to engage in similar unlawful activities were also taken into consideration,” police added.

Parliamentary opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, from the Congress party, backed the men, who were detained after entering the site.

Jantar Mantar, in the heart of the capital, has been sealed off for days with yellow metal barricades and guarded by security personnel.

Delhi Police said on Monday it had removed the site from the list of designated protest venues.

‘Stand up’

“Waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime,” Gandhi said in a post on social media. “Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice.” The Congress and CJP have both organised protests over the voter roll revision. Gandhi said on Wednesday that “all protests are one”.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke praised the men, saying they “knew they could be thrown behind bars” but went ahead to wave the national flag.

“They’ve shown the entire country that the only way to stand up to a bully like Modi is to never bow down, no matter the consequences,” he said in a post on X.

Das has worked as a journalist, while Ranka, an engineer, studied at the prestigious Indian Institute of Technology and the London School of Economics.

Rights advocates and critics say Modi’s government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents – allegations the government rejects.

Human Rights Watch said Wednesday the Indian government must uphold the right of citizens to protest peacefully.

“The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections,” it said in a statement.

One of the protesters, who gave only her first name, said Wednesday she was taken to a detention centre where she was beaten by police.

‘Unacceptable’

“They punched me here,” said Atira, pointing to her face at a news conference in Delhi, standing next to Gandhi.

“I begged them to stop, but then they started kicking me in my private parts, lower abdomen, and back. They didn’t consider me as a human.” AFP could not immediately verify her claim.

Journalists in New Delhi marched on Tuesday to protest the detention of reporters during demonstrations. The Press Club of India said any attacks on journalists doing their jobs were “unacceptable”.

The electoral list revision, which began last year, has led to more than 133 million names being removed from voter rolls, according to media reports.

Critics say the exercise has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.

Election authorities say the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

Home Minister Amit Shah, Modi’s powerful right-hand man, dismissed the protests as localised and accused Gandhi of pursuing an “action plan to protect infiltrators”.

“The people of India are not going to fall for your deception,” he said, predicting a “resounding majority” for government in the next general election, due in 2029.

item.title: State-owned company plans satellite surveillance in the Bay of Bengal at a cost of Tk 6b
item.description:
The government aims to establish a satellite-based surveillance system to detect the location of fishing vessels in the Bay of Bengal, monitor sea traffic, and gather information on illegal activities.

For this purpose, Bangladesh Satellite Company Limited (BSCL) plans to use an upgraded version of the Automatic Identification System (AIS).

Officials from the organisation state that this surveillance will be conducted through four low-altitude satellites. The estimated cost of the project could be around Tk 6 billion.

Bangladesh’s first satellite, Bangabandhu Satellite-1, was launched in 2018. It primarily functions for signal exchange and broadcasting from space. BSCL's proposed maritime surveillance system will be designed for different technical purposes. Currently, feasibility studies for the project are underway.

Experts say that the Automatic Identification System, or AIS, primarily facilitates the exchange of information regarding a vessel’s identity, location, speed, and course. In the conventional system, this information is received through coastal radio infrastructure.

In a satellite-based AIS system, signals from vessels at sea can be received via satellites, allowing their movement to be tracked from remote locations.

However, this system will only provide information for those vessels equipped with appropriate devices that can receive signals.

4 satellites, 2 ground stations

After resolving maritime boundary disputes with Myanmar in 2012 and India in 2014, Bangladesh acquired rights over 118, 813 square kilometers in the Bay of Bengal.

Government officials state that effective monitoring is necessary for fishing, vessel movement, and the utilisation of marine resources in this vast sea area.

BSCL's documents propose four satellites, two ground stations, and local server infrastructure for data processing to facilitate this surveillance. The goal is to achieve a maximum 'revisit time' of 30 minutes over the entire Bay of Bengal area. This means the interval between satellite observations in a particular area will be 30 minutes.

BSCL sources say they plan to use local servers for data processing and storage within the country. The aim is to maintain control over marine data at the national level and reduce dependence on foreign third parties.

When asked, BSCL's Managing Director (MD) Muhammad Imadur Rahman told Prothom Alo that they aim to complete the feasibility study by October. Afterward, the technical specifications of the project will be finalised, and an international tender to hire a manufacturing company will be announced. If a decision is made within this year, completion by 2028 is possible.

Emergency communications

According to the information from the international fisheries research organisation WorldFish’s ECOFISH-2 Activity, funded by USAID, more than 5 million people's primary source of income in the coastal area is marine fish resources.

Additionally, incidents such as trawler sinkings in the Bay of Bengal, resulting in fishermen's deaths, and being swept away into foreign waters by waves occur frequently. Fishing trawlers often lack navigational equipment. Fishermen use the stars to navigate in the deep sea. If caught in a storm, they may drift into foreign territories.

According to the ‘Fish Safe 2025’ project information from the UK-based international charity Lloyd's Register Foundation, working on fishermen''s safety, over 1,350 fishermen die in the sea annually in Bangladesh due to the lack of safety equipment.

Acting Director of the Marine Fisheries Department of the Fisheries Directorate, Md Nazrul Islam, told Prothom Alo that a satellite-based surveillance system is needed for monitoring fishing vessels at sea. It will make it easier to detect vessel locations and ensure compliance with fishing regulations.

Md Nazrul Islam stated that although there are existing rules for fishing beyond a specified depth, some vessels do not comply. Coordinating vessel location information with relevant departments and checkpoints will aid in law enforcement and oversight.

Detecting illegal vessel movements

BSCL states that using information about vessel locations and movements to plan voyages can reduce unnecessary travel by fishermen, leading to fuel savings.

The organisation has provided an estimate for fuel savings. According to their calculations, a boat can save up to 150 liters of diesel per trip if traveling as planned. Annually, this would result in a total fuel saving of 45 million liters, valued at Tk 4.59 billion.

According to the Fisheries Directorate, approximately 30,000 small or artisanal fishing boats are registered in the country. Additionally, the directorate estimates there are at least another 70,000 unregistered boats. BSCL suggests that satellite surveillance will make it easier to identify illegal vessels.

However, experts warn that identifying vessels lacking AIS equipment or those that intentionally turn off the device is challenging with the conventional AIS system. Therefore, questions remain about how many types of vessels can be detected with the proposed system and whether any other technology will be necessary for surveillance.

When asked, Professor Mohammad Atiquzzaman from the School of Computer Science at the University of Oklahoma, USA, told Prothom Alo that technologies like Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) should be used alongside AIS, allowing the detection of vessels not transmitting AIS signals.

Satellite expert Atiquzzaman also emphasises the importance of thoroughly evaluating the technical and economic feasibility of the project before investing.

Atiquzzaman states that it must be examined whether the required area can be monitored with four satellites. Additionally, analyzing the project's cost-benefit ratio and whether obtaining similar services from international satellite operators would be more economical is necessary.

item.title: Special tribunals for expatriates planned at divisional level: Law minister
item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman on Tuesday said the government plans to establish specialised tribunals at divisional headquarters to ensure speedy disposal of cases involving expatriates.

"Expatriates often face years of harassment over legal disputes involving property purchased with money sent from abroad or the recovery of money sent to family members in Bangladesh.

The proposed tribunals would deal exclusively with cases involving expatriates to reduce their suffering and ensure faster justice," the law minister said.

Fresh blow to overseas employment in Saudi Arabia

He made the remarks while addressing the inaugural session of the 'Shonar Manush Sammilon-2026', organised by the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU) at a hotel in the capital to mark the organisation's 30th anniversary.

Md Asaduzzaman said the proposal is currently at the drafting stage. Recalling his recent visit to Dubai, the law minister said Bangladeshi migrant workers there lead extremely difficult lives.

Despite enduring such gruelling conditions, Bangladeshi workers receive much lower wages than workers from other countries, he said, urging the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment to look into the matter seriously.

Saudi Arabia urges timely renewal of expatriate work permits

Blaming unscrupulous recruiting agencies for one of the major challenges facing expatriates, Asaduzzaman said 5,000 visas had already been cancelled in the Middle East, particularly in the United Arab Emirates, while many more were awaiting cancellation.

Explaining the reasons, he said many recruiting agencies were submitting fake certificates and documents that did not even exist.

 As the authenticity of such documents can now be easily verified using artificial intelligence (AI), the countries concerned are taking legal action against those involved, the law minister added.

BB introduces new account facility for expatriate Bangladeshis

Praising RMMRU for its 30-year journey, Md Asaduzzaman said, "We believe that RMMRU and its team have never been involved in any activity contrary to the interests of workers. No one has alleged that RMMRU misappropriated funds collected in workers' names. We have seen no corruption in RMMRU's integrity. We have never seen RMMRU engaging in sycophancy."

At the event, he expressed hope that RMMRU's 30-year journey would extend into the next 100 years, helping build a Bangladesh where migrant workers would return home to work, and the country would recruit workers from abroad.

item.description:
Former three-time MP and BNP Commerce Affairs Secretary Salahuddin Ahmed died at a hospital in the capital on Tuesday night. He was 80.

He breathed his last at Evercare Hospital Dhaka at 8:10pm, his son Tanvir Ahmed Robin, member secretary of Dhaka South City BNP, told UNB.

Robin said his father's namaz-e-janaza will be held after Zohr prayers at Lal Mosque in Shyampur-Kadamtali on Wednesday. He urged all to pray for the salvation of his father's departed soul.

Salahuddin Ahmed was elected MP from the Dhaka-4 and Dhaka-5 constituencies as a BNP candidate in the 1991, February 1996 and 2001 parliamentary elections.

He contested the June 1996, 2008 and 2018 national elections but was defeated.

During the 2018 parliamentary election, he was seriously injured in a knife attack while protesting alleged irregularities in the voting.

A former general secretary of undivided Dhaka city BNP, Salahuddin had been suffering from age-related illnesses for several years.

He was recently admitted to Evercare Hospital with lung problems and other complications.

item.title: SSC students failing up to two subjects will be able to retake exams within 15 days: Edu minister
item.description:
Students who fail in up to two subjects in the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examinations will be allowed to retake those exams within 15 days of the publication of results, Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon has said.

He made the announcement today, Tuesday, at the opening ceremony of an orientation training course for officers of the 49th BCS General Education Cadre at the Rural Development Academy in Bogura.

Speaking as the chief guest, the minister said, “What we will do for the SSC examinations is this: those who fail in a maximum of two subjects will sit the exams again within 15 days. We will not carry the legacy of failure forward year after year.”

SSC, HSC: Education boards ready to hold re-exams in failed subjects within 3 months

He said a decision on whether the students would remain in general education would be made based on the results of the retake examinations. Those who fail to pass the retake examinations would be transferred to technical education.

At present, students who fail in one or more subjects in public examinations such as the SSC and HSC must sit the exams again the following year. They can retake only the subjects they failed or, if they wish, sit all the subjects again.

However, students who fail in just one or two subjects have to wait a full year, which can set back their education and create additional mental stress.

HSC results to be published between 25 and 29 October

Against this backdrop, students, guardians and education stakeholders have been calling for a system allowing students to retake failed subjects within three months of the publication of results.

Last Saturday, the Campaign for Popular Education (CAMPE) organised a conference for students who failed the SSC and equivalent examinations at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in the capital.

Students from different areas shared their problems and feelings at the event, where they called for retakes in failed subjects within three months of the publication of results.

At the same event, Mahdi Amin, the prime minister’s adviser on education, said the government was also considering the proposal positively.

SSC in January, HSC in June from next academic year

He said the government would give positive consideration to allowing students who fail one or more subjects in public examinations such as the SSC to retake only those subjects within three months, rather than wait a year.

However, he also noted that introducing the system for this year’s SSC examinations might be difficult.

On Monday, the education boards submitted their opinions to the Ministry of Education, saying students could be allowed to retake failed subjects within three months of the publication of SSC and HSC results.

However, they said such retakes could be arranged for this year’s HSC and equivalent examinations, but not for this year’s SSC and equivalent examinations.

Why so many errors in answer-sheet evaluation? Questions raised over assessment method

According to the boards, the system could be introduced for the SSC examinations from next year.

The education minister has now said students who fail in up to two subjects will be able to retake those exams within 15 days.

Educationists, as well as current and former chairmen of education boards, also believe the boards can arrange such examinations, if a policy decision is made. This would spare students from having to wait a year.

It would also reduce complications involving the simultaneous examination of regular and irregular candidates, as well as the preparation and distribution of question papers for them, they added.

item.title: Saudi crown prince moved between fortified palaces amid Houthi attacks
item.description:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is being moved between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers as Houthi attacks intensify, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal cited by The Independent.
The reported security measures come after a deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday that killed 13 people and injured at least 300, marking Saudi Arabia’s worst attack in a decade, according to the report.
The 41-year-old crown prince has not appeared in public since Tuesday, when he participated in a national blood donation campaign. Officials familiar with his movements told the Wall Street Journal that he has since been staying at fortified palaces under the protection of a handpicked security team.
The Saudi foreign ministry did not immediately respond to The Independent’s request for comment.
The Houthis have reiterated their intention to target Saudi airports. King Khalid International Airport, which has reportedly been struck four times in five days, has remained closed since the weekend missile attack.
Around 60% of scheduled flights at the Riyadh airport were expected to be cancelled on Monday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said the kingdom’s response would be “equally serious”, reflecting the gravity of the attacks.
Saudi officials have also warned that the kingdom is running low on missile interceptors needed to defend against further strikes.
Last month, Riyadh sought air defense assistance from France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt, officials told The Associated Press. One official noted that the United States had also seen its interceptor stockpiles decline during the war involving Iran.
The latest escalation comes amid renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement, following the breakdown of a fragile ceasefire agreed in 2022.
The Houthis resumed attacks after accusing Saudi Arabia of targeting Sanaa airport while an Iranian aircraft was attempting to land.
US President Donald Trump has said he is considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis, while Riyadh’s allies in the Mecca Pact have expressed support for the kingdom.
Iranian military spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran was deeply concerned about developments in the Arabian Peninsula, warning that the fighting would benefit Israel.
Saudi and Iranian foreign ministers also spoke late Sunday as tensions escalated. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned against relying on military action while ignoring the political situation and said Tehran would help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government, beginning years of conflict with the Houthi movement.

item.title: IMF boosts this year’s global economy growth outlook, but warns of risks from AI and debt
item.description:
The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday slightly upgraded its outlook for the world economy for this year, while warning of growing risks from rising debt, including the financial frenzy around artificial intelligence.

The IMF says it expects the global economy to grow at a 3.1% pace this year. That’s up from its July forecast for 3.0% growth and well below the 3.5% expansion in 2025. Growth in 2027 should rebound to 3.4%, it said in its latest Economic Outlook.

The report, released as world economic and financial leaders gathered in Bangkok for the fall meetings of the IMF and World Bank, predicts that growth in the United States will remain steady at 2.3% in 2026 and 2027.

Collectively, advanced economies will grow 2.1% this year, up from 2.0% in 2025, and then slow to 1.9% growth next year, it said.

The forecasts are based on a nearly 41% increase in oil prices this year, at an average of $96 a barrel. Global inflation is foreseen at 4.7% in 2026, falling to 4.1% next year. They are also based on the assumption that shipments of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz will resume by March, and that the boom in AI demand will moderate.

AI has uneven impacts

The boom in artificial intelligence is offsetting damage from sharply higher prices for oil and gas, IMF economists say, but it also carries risks.

Its benefits are not shared equally: The U.S. and China account for more than three-quarters of net demand for imports of computer chips and other AI-related equipment, the report said.

“The outlook is highly uneven,” Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s director of research, told reporters in Bangkok.

Growth is increasingly concentrated, with 32 countries accounting for 95% of global growth, the report said. That compares with 54 countries as of April.

“The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength,” it says.

Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director at the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said an AI-related correction in stock markets is just one of the risks. Rising bond yields are another evolving problem, along with cyberthreats that could disrupt financial systems, he said.

Underscoring such concerns, sell-offs of AI-related shares swept through Asia on Tuesday, with South Korea’s Kospi sinking as much as 7% before it closed 5.5% lower.

AI’s effects on employment are another worry, “a slow moving tsunami, but a tsunami nonetheless,” IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said.

“The impact over time on jobs globally we estimate to be around 40%—jobs either augmented or downgraded or eliminated. And we are already seeing some of this impact,” she said.

Debt remains a key concern for regional economies

The IMF chief is urging countries to do a better job of improving their national finances and taming mounting levels of debt.

That’s especially crucial at a time of high borrowing costs, Tenreyro said.

Countries that are somewhat insulated from the energy shocks of the Iran war and that are benefiting from rapid adoption of AI are managing to keep growth on track. But developing economies and emerging markets more vulnerable to higher costs for oil and gas will see growth slow to 3.7% this year from 4.5% in 2025, the report says. It forecasts they will regain momentum next year, expanding at a 4.4% annual pace.

The situation is much worse in the Middle East and Central Asia, where those regions’ economies are expected to contract this year before recovering to a 6.3% rate of growth in 2027.

The 21 European countries that share the euro currency are expected to grow by a meager 1.1% this year and 1.2% in 2027.

China, the world’s No. 2 economy, is expected to expand 4.5% this year, down from 5% in 2025, in line with the government’s official target.

India is once again forecast to be the world’s fastest-growing major economy, advancing at a 7% clip, down from a sizzling 7.7% last year.

The IMF is a 191-nation lending organization that works to promote economic growth and financial stability and to reduce global poverty. At the meetings in Bangkok, finance ministers and central bank governors will assess the state of the world economy and discuss strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth.

—By Elaine Kurtenbach, AP business writer

Associated Press journalists Haruka Nuga and Tian Macleod Ji contributed.

item.title: Getty Images was worth $4.8 billion just 4 years ago. Now it’s filing for bankruptcy
item.description:
Getty Images is filing for bankruptcy and plans to go private, the company announced on Monday.A release says that the company plans to begin the process of filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the weeks ahead and undergo massive restructuring, which will ultimately see complete control and ownership of the company in the hands of the Getty family, as well as Koch Equity Development.

As a part of the restructuring, Koch Equity Development (which is the investment arm of Koch, Inc.) will invest up to $533 million, and as the process progresses, the company will “continue to operate in the normal course,” and “vendors will be unaffected and paid in full in the ordinary course of business,” according to the company’s release.

Getty is perhaps best known as a source of photographs and stock images used for a variety of purposes, and has faced significant headwinds with the advent of AI-generated imagery in recent years. Notably, in a recent investor presentation, company materials noted that there was “declining agency demand and disruption to the iStock eCommerce business. It had also announced plans to merge with Shutterstock in January—a plan that has since been scrapped.

Even so, company leadership says that it’s confident that going private and restructuring will help it regain its footing.

Mark Getty, Getty Images’ co-founder and chairman of the board, said in the company release that he was “pleased to continue our strong partnership with Koch Equity Development and the lender groups to provide capital structure improvements that will enable us to build on our solid foundation and seize new growth opportunities.”

Additionally, Mike Harris, senior managing director and co-head at Koch Equity Development, said that the group remains “confident in the company’s future and fully support this transaction alongside the Getty family. This equity investment will provide Getty Images with a firm financial foundation and greater flexibility to continue investing in its employees, customers, contributors, and future growth.”

item.title: Bumble stock soars as the embattled dating app strikes deal to go private. Here’s how it got here
item.description:
Bumble has spent the past few years trying everything from a new CEO to AI-powered matches. 

Now, the embattled dating app company is making another big move: going private.

Ithaca Holdings, a new firm run by former tech executives, is acquiring Bumble for $1.3 billion, the latter announced on Tuesday. Bumble’s board unanimously voted in favor of the deal, with founder and CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd recusing herself from the decision. 

News of a potential deal was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Bumble’s shareholders will receive $6.05 for each share of Class A Common Stock. According to Bumble, this is about 138% higher than its Friday, October 9, closing share price and around 119% over its 30-day weighted average price ending Friday. 

The dating app company was valued at about $335 million at the end of business on Friday. 

Ithaca’s co-CEOs and co-founders, Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, will take over as co-CEOs of Bumble and “partner with Wolfe Herd to extend Bumble’s original vision to help people find connections in life and love into the next era.” 

For anyone wondering what this arrangement might look like, this line in the announcement provides a pretty good idea: “Ithaca’s mission is to apply frontier technology to renew and accelerate businesses that enrich people’s lives and create lasting value in a world transformed by AI.” 

Blackstone, which owns a stake in Bumble, has approved the deal.

Wolfe Herd sang Ithaca’s praises, stating, “In Ithaca, we have found a partner who shares our vision, believes in our women-first mission, and is committed to investing in Bumble’s future.”

Bumble’s journey as a public company

Bumble went public in February 2021, making founder and CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd the youngest woman to take a company public or become a self-made billionaire. It was a success story. 

However, in the five-plus years since, the company has struggled to stay relevant in a world that has grown increasingly tired of dating apps. 

As of October 5, shares of Bumble Inc. (Nasdaq: BMBL) were down almost 95% from their opening high. The stock has had a relatively steady decline over its half a decade of trading. 

That all changed on Monday when news broke of a potential sale. While still over $80 lower than its record high, Bumble’s shares closed up 49.61%. As of publication, the stock has been fluctuating close to 4% up during premarket trading. 

Attempts to stay relevant in recent years

Dating apps of all shapes and sizes have faced a decline as Gen Z, in particular, moves away from online dating. Match Group-owned Hinge is a notable exception to the trend.

Wolfe Herd stepped down as CEO in January 2024, transitioning to the position of executive chair. Her successor, Lidiane Jones—a former Slack CEO—soon cut about 350 roles. 

Jones’s tenure didn’t last very long, with Wolfe Herd returning as CEO in March 2025.

A few months later, Bumble cut another 240 positions, about 30% of its workforce. Shortly after, Wolfe Herd threatened to remove “members with low-quality and incomplete profiles” in a focus on quality over quantity. 

Bumble has also paid attention to its non-romantic ventures. In November 2025, the company launched a new standalone BFF app.

Like many tech CEOs, Wolfe Herd has turned to AI as a potential draw for users. In May, Bumble launched an AI assistant called Bee. Bumble calls Bee a matchmaker, with the tool meant to replace the need to swipe. The company is also testing out having Bee create dates for matches. 

Then, in August, Bumble announced it would be getting rid of its distinguishing feature: women messaging first. 

The company cited a 2024 internal survey that found two-thirds of women felt less pressure around dating when men made the first move. At the time, the company launched its Opening Move feature, which allowed men to make the first move using preset prompts and gave women 24 hours to respond or the match expired. 

Now, anyone can message and users have 72 hours to respond. 

“Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides,” Wolfe Herd said in the announcement. “This evolution isn’t a departure from our founding vision, but the realization of it.”

item.title: Character.ai has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection as it moves to sell assets to Disney
item.description:
Controversial chatbot platform Character.ai is seeking Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the wake of mounting legal challenges and runaway operating costs, the four-year-old startup said in a surprise announcement on Monday.

The move comes as the Menlo Park, California, company has faced a number of lawsuits in recent years, including some that say its AI companions have encouraged users to harm or kill themselves.

In its announcement, Character.ai said it has reached an agreement with Disney Worldwide Services, an affiliate of the Walt Disney Company, to sell some of its intellectual property for $20 million and “transition services” that will help Character.ai continue to operate, at least temporarily.

Disney will serve as a “stalking horse” bidder in the Chapter 11 proceedings, meaning other companies could offer competing bids.

Fast Company reached out to Disney for comment.

“Over the past year, Character.ai has taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve its business in the face of significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” CEO Colin Adams said in a statement. “After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the Company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders.”

In a blog post, the company said its platform “remains up and running” as it seeks to figure out a path forward. It expects the sale process to be completed by November or early December.

The Pentagon’s Drone Revolution Starts With Soldiers
item.description:
Welcome to The Iron Triangle, the Cipher Brief column serving Procurement Officers tasked with buying the future, Investors funding the next generation of defense technology, and the Policy Wonks analyzing its impact on the global order.

On the night of April 24, 1980, eight Navy RH-53D Sea Stallions lifted off the deck of the USS Nimitz and headed for a patch of Iranian salt flat called Desert One. The plan needed six of them to get there in working order. One was abandoned in the desert after a rotor warning. One turned back in a dust storm. One arrived with a failed hydraulic system. The mission was aborted. Then, while the force repositioned to refuel, a helicopter drifted into an EC-130. Eight Americans died on that salt flat, and fifty-two hostages stayed in Tehran.

When the Secretary of War stood at Quantico on September 30 and announced a new four-star command for autonomous warfare, my first question was not about drones. It was about helicopters.

The Holloway review found the mission "conceptually valid and feasible" and blamed "the ad hoc nature of the organization and planning." The fix, Nunn-Cohen in 1986, gave the new Special Operations Command a budget line the services could not raid. We did eventually build better helicopter units. But we didn't build SOCOM around a helicopter. We built it around the problem that broke the helicopters.

The Secretary seems to understand this. "Ukraine's lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars," Hegseth told the room, "but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt." His signed memo says the output "is not a particular drone, but the ability to adapt in combat." Then the Department named it the Autonomous Warfare Command. This is like naming SOCOM the Helicopter Command. A drone is a photograph of an adaptation. The adaptation is the movie. In Ukraine, radio-controlled FPVs gave way to fiber-optic spools, which gave way to nets, shotguns and interceptor drones, each turn in weeks or months.

When the 3rd Army Corps air-dropped ground robots ten kilometers behind Russian lines during Operation Vivaldi last month, the footage went everywhere. The commanders talked about something else. A battalion commander known as "Darwin," credited a command structure "qualified enough as we are." An American volunteer with the corps described his entire job as "installing Western mission command trust and initiative." We taught them that. They are teaching it back to us with robots, and we are taking notes on the robots.

Retired Lt. Gen. Mark Hertling warns that "creating a headquarters does not create a capability." He is right, and that is the point of this column. The memo orders a 30-day implementation plan, due on the Secretary's desk around the end of October. A headquarters is a wiring diagram. The capability is a soldier in the motor pool at two in the morning with a soldering iron, a laptop and a firmware image that does not work yet. Here is how to build him, keep him and turn him loose.

Start With the Soldier We Already Have

The Army has made a great start. Its newest specialty, the 15X tactical unmanned aircraft system specialist, is graduating classes of about thirty at Fort Huachuca, with 770 expected by year's end and a planned force of two to three thousand. The colonel who runs the training brigade said it better than anyone at Quantico: "The Army has not bought a drone that the 15X is responsible for being an expert on." Train the soldier to learn the machine, not the machine's manual.

Now follow that soldier for six years. If he is good, he makes sergeant. If he is very good, he makes staff sergeant, and the day he pins it on, his job stops being the drone and starts being the eight soldiers who fly it: counseling, evaluations, ranges and the duty roster. The enlisted promotion system has one ladder, and it runs through the leadership of people. The best technician in the platoon either becomes a manager or gets passed over. Either way he leaves the bench, and the private sector is waiting with a better offer.

Bring Back the Specialist

Warrant officers exist to solve part of this problem. The Army already has an unmanned aircraft systems warrant, and the Air Force, which abolished its warrants in 1959, brought them back in December 2024 for cyber, intelligence and space. But warrants are a thin layer by design. You do not put one in every platoon, and the loop the Secretary described lives in the squad and the section.

The Army has solved this before. In 1955, after a committee recommended separating command from technical responsibility, it created specialist grades to reward experience and technical knowledge. A Specialist Six drew a staff sergeant's pay without a staff sergeant's squad. His job was to be the most technically proficient in the building, and the Army paid him to stay that way. The ladder was dismantled from the top down, and in 1985 SP5 and SP6 went away.

Bring them back, starting with unmanned systems. Promote a Specialist Five or Six on what he can build, fix, modify and teach. Same pay grades, separate ladder, one rule: technical authority, never command. Put specialists in every formation that flies, drives or swims a robot, with the warrant corps above them as the technical chain. A Specialist Six at battalion who can rewrite the flight controller tonight, and a CW3 at brigade who knows which vendor to call in the morning: that is what a fix in days looks like.

Pay for the Skill, Not the Stripe

We already pay soldiers for perishable expertise. A linguist earns a Foreign Language Proficiency Bonus of up to $500 a month per language, and must retest every year to keep it. Nobody thinks that is strange. Russian is hard, and it fades.

So does firmware. Build a tiered certification for unmanned systems (repair, modify, program) and pay it monthly, with an annual retest, because the skill expires as fast as the drones do. The money does not need an act of Congress. Under 37 U.S.C. 353, a service Secretary can designate any skill as critical and pay up to $1,750 a month in skill incentive pay, or a proficiency bonus of up to $55,000 a year for certified proficiency. The authority is sitting on the shelf.

Then add the cheapest incentive in the Army's inventory: a badge. The 1953 committee that produced the specialist grades was worried about prestige, and prestige in the Army is worn on the chest. Anyone who has watched soldiers grind through an Expert Infantryman Badge lane knows what they will do for a piece of metal. An expert badge for unmanned systems, tested on build, fix and fly against the clock, would cost almost nothing and fill every off-duty hour in the brigade.

Recruit at the Bench

In June 2025, the Army commissioned four technology executives directly as reserve lieutenant colonels. Now do it at the other end of the org chart. Let a civilian FPV builder or embedded-systems engineer enlist as a Specialist Five instead of a private, on a skills test rather than a resume.

And stop leaving the best reservoir untapped. Thousands of Americans now build drones for a living. The Guard and Reserve can put them in uniform one weekend a month as technical specialists, carrying current industry skill into units without the Army having to match a Silicon Valley salary.

Give Them Permission and a Parts Budget

A specialist who can fix the drone but is not allowed to innovate is an expensive spectator. In April 2025 the Secretary's own Army transformation memo directed the service to "seek to include right to repair provisions in all existing contracts." Finish the job, then delegate the authority to modify and fly small systems down to brigade, so a fix written tonight does not wait months for a distant office to approve it.

Then give him money. The Army's UAS Marketplace, launched in March, has already cleared more than $750 million in sales, and it is adding components and software. Ukraine went further: drone units earn points for verified strikes and spend them on the Brave1 Market, a catalog of more than a thousand products. We do not need the kill leaderboard. We need the principle. Put a parts budget and a catalog in the hands of the battalion specialist, because the fix usually costs less than the paperwork.

Train the Whole Chain

Technical acumen cannot stop at the specialist. The lieutenant has to know what to ask for, and the battalion commander has to know when a twenty-year-old is telling him something he does not want to hear. Put a hands-on unmanned systems block in the officer basic and captains career courses. Send specialists to vendor factories through Training With Industry, and bring vendor engineers forward to battalion in return. Then rate commanders on how fast their formations close the loop.

For the Procurement Officer

Before you sign, ask one question: can a twenty-two-year-old with a screwdriver and a laptop legally open this, fix it and reflash it at two in the morning? If the answer is a field service rep and a ticket number, you did not buy a capability. You rented one. Price the technical data, the open interfaces and the soldier training as line items, and count how many of your fielded systems a Specialist Six could actually work on today.

The Investment Thesis

Your next customer is a Specialist Six. Buying power is already drifting down to the units, through marketplaces here and points in Ukraine. The company with the best drone of 2026 is a commodity supplier by 2027. The company the soldier chooses to learn on, train on and fix with is a platform. Discount revenue built on dependency, and pay up for iteration speed.

The Policy Wonk's Warning

The memo says plainly that the Department will need legislation for the command itself. When the FY2028 NDAA takes it up, Congress should do for adaptation what Nunn-Cohen did for special operations: a protected budget line, and a statutory charter that defines the mission as adaptation across the force, not ownership of a category of hardware. Most of the personnel fixes above need no new law at all. Congress's job is to ask why they have not happened yet.

My Take.

The fight over this command will happen in a document most people will never read. The 30-day plan must "identify measures of adaptation and Service adoption." That clause is where AUTOWARCOM is won or lost. If adaptation is measured in drones delivered, the command becomes a very expensive purchasing agent. Measure two numbers instead: days from a unit reporting a battlefield problem to a fix in its hands, and the count of soldiers in each formation certified to make that fix. Report both to Congress every quarter. Owen West and Max Strasiser built their reputations on speed. I suspect they would welcome being graded on it.

The Risk.

The specialist ranks went away for reasons. Old soldiers still tell stories about the Spec Five who drew sergeant's pay and could not, or would not, run a detail, and about the confusion over who was in charge when the sergeant went down. The bright line between technical authority and command answers most of that. Delegating authority to modify means some soldiers will break drones. That is the tuition, and it is cheaper than the alternative. The bigger risk is the one Hertling named: a new headquarters that adds a layer between the operator and the vendor. If the 30-day plan is mostly wiring diagram and very little soldier, believe him.

Conclusion

Hegseth told the room at Quantico that the English at Agincourt moved their fletchers close to the front to keep the arrows coming. The fletchers were not archers. They were tradesmen, kept near the line because the arrows ran out faster than anyone had planned. In a few weeks, the plan on the Secretary's desk will tell us whether we understood the story. Will we count drones, or will we count days, and the soldiers who make them shorter?

item.title: The Yemen war is not just Saudi Arabia’s problem. It’s the Gulf’s too
item.description:
The Yemen war is not just Saudi Arabia’s problem. It’s the Gulf’s too Expert comment thilton.drupal 14 October 2026

The renewed conflict in Yemen exposes the limits of Saudi Arabia’s military options and the vulnerabilities of the Gulf states. A unified Gulf Cooperation Council strategy on Yemen and a credible political settlement between Yemenis are needed.

The Yemen conflict has escalated significantly in recent weeks. Houthi strikes on airports in Riyadh, Abha and Dammam have killed at least 20 people and injured hundreds. Saudi oil infrastructure has also been attacked. Within Yemen, renewed fighting following a Houthi offensive around the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait has brought return to full-scale war. 

The escalation is an alarming reminder of the 2015 Saudi-led intervention in Yemen. This came after the Iran-backed Houthis seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in September 2014 and ousted the internationally recognized government from power. More than a decade later, the Houthis remain entrenched and clearly emboldened, while Yemen’s government is fragmented. Prospects for a political settlement currently seem remote. 

Since the UN-brokered truce in April 2022, Saudi Arabia has sought to disengage militarily from Yemen and pursue a negotiated settlement with the Houthis. Talks gained momentum in 2023, but the Houthis’ involvement in the Gaza war, including attacks on Red Sea shipping and Israel, disrupted the political process. US president Donald Trump’s intensive bombing campaign against the Houthis led to a separate US-Houthi ceasefire in May 2025. But it did not advance solutions to the conflict in Yemen.

Difficult choices for Riyadh

Saudi Arabia now faces a difficult choice between flawed options.

The first option is military escalation through renewed air strikes and an offensive by Yemeni government-aligned forces. But this risks returning Riyadh to the costly, ill-planned and ill-conducted war it has spent years attempting to extricate itself from. 

The Houthis have learned that even limited strikes can impose disproportionate economic and political costs. This gives the group leverage that Saudi Arabia’s conventional military superiority has struggled to overcome.

Seeking to contain the Houthis has also proved insufficient. Although the relative calm following the 2022 truce reduced cross-border attacks, it allowed the Houthis to consolidate their territorial control and strengthen their military capabilities, only to attack Saudi Arabia again.

Negotiation remains the most favourable route towards a lasting settlement. But it faces a fundamental obstacle: the Houthis believe they are winning and have little incentive to compromise.

Nor can Riyadh simply outsource the conflict. The US faces the looming prospect of a renewed confrontation with Iran and is therefore unlikely to have much appetite for opening another front or supporting a prolonged military campaign in Yemen. Saudi Arabia’s defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan may strengthen deterrence and defensive capabilities, but it does not offer a solution to the Houthi threat or Yemen’s underlying political fragmentation.

Saudi Arabia cannot win this war alone, but neither can it outsource its resolution. The lesson of the past decade is that military pressure without a coherent political strategy will only reproduce the conditions that allowed the Houthis to consolidate their position.

A Gulf problem

Instead, a collective Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) response is needed. Yemen and the Houthis have become a collective Gulf security challenge. It would therefore be a mistake to continue treating Yemen primarily as a domestic conflict or a Saudi security problem. 

The attacks on Saudi airports have further demonstrated the vulnerability of critical infrastructure across the GCC to missiles, drones and other asymmetric threats. This exposure is not confined to Saudi Arabia. In January 2022, the Houthis launched attacks on Abu Dhabi’s oil facilities and airport, killing three people and injuring six. This threat is particularly concerning for the Gulf states as most of their economic diversification agendas depend on secure aviation, logistics, tourism, investment and a stable regional environment.

Attacks on Saudi transport infrastructure also threaten the wider Gulf by disrupting vital supply routes. The kingdom’s extensive land connections have become increasingly important and provided alternative supply routes for neighbouring GCC states while the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted. 

Yemen’s economic collapse, water scarcity and demographic pressures also make its stability a long-term Gulf interest. 

The GCC must therefore move beyond expressing support for Saudi Arabia. It should pursue a coordinated strategy that creates a unified GCC agenda directed at strengthening Yemen’s government and establishing a credible political pathway to ending the conflict.

Gulf unity must go beyond condemnation

A collective Gulf response must begin by addressing the divisions that have undermined previous efforts in Yemen. Most importantly, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) must move beyond their damaging confrontation over southern Yemen in early 2026. Despite entering the 2015 intervention as allies, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi have increasingly pursued competing priorities and supported rival Yemeni factions.

Reconciliation requires more than expressions of solidarity following Houthi attacks. The UAE should reconsider its support for southern separatist ambitions and work towards a unified but decentralized Yemen that accommodates southern grievances and competing political interests.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, must reassess its dependence on established Yemeni partners, particularly the Islah Party, whose alleged Muslim Brotherhood connections have long generated Emirati opposition. Riyadh’s reliance on Islah-linked networks has narrowed its political options and contributed to divisions within the anti-Houthi camp.

Both countries must recognize that their competing relationships with Yemeni factions have weakened the very forces they seek to support. Without agreement on Yemen’s political future, renewed military coordination will achieve little.

Gulf coordination must also be matched by a serious reassessment of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

The Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), established in 2022 to replace former president Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi, was intended to unite competing anti-Houthi factions. Yet years of internal rivalries, weak governance, and limited institutional accountability, as well as alleged widespread corruption, have undermined its effectiveness.

Saudi Arabia should continue providing financial support to sustain basic services and prevent economic collapse in government-controlled areas. But this backing should go to the government and cabinet, not the PLC.  

The experience of the Hadi presidency serves as a clear warning that a decade of backing an ineffective leadership did little to strengthen the Yemeni state or reverse Houthi gains. Today, Riyadh cannot afford to repeat that mistake.

A more effective governance structure is essential not only to strengthen the position of anti-Houthi forces but also to provide a credible Yemeni counterpart in any future political settlement.  

Towards a larger Gulf–Yemeni settlement

Although Saudi-Emirati reconciliation is indispensable, a sustainable Gulf strategy must also involve Qatar and Oman.

Qatar should contribute to a more coherent Gulf political approach in Yemen, including through its media influence and relationships with Yemeni actors. Oman, meanwhile, should retain its role as a diplomatic intermediary. Muscat’s channels with the Houthis and preference for mediation make it particularly well placed to facilitate future negotiations without joining military operations.

Related work

Why the Houthis’ Red Sea power play makes Iran even stronger

The ultimate objective should be a Gulf-backed political settlement that preserves a unified but decentralized Yemen and accommodates its competing political constituencies. All factions, including the Houthis, should be able to participate, conditional on verifiable commitments to relinquish heavy weapons and accept a common political framework. This would require sustained Gulf diplomatic and financial support.

After more than a decade of war, the Houthis still control Sanaa, Yemen’s government remains weak and Gulf divisions continue to undermine efforts to end the conflict. Avoiding another prolonged war requires a common Gulf vision, investment in a functioning Yemeni government and a political settlement that addresses the causes of the conflict, rather than merely seeking to contain its consequences.
